chunks: Amir al-Mu'minin عليه السلام heard a man saying, “The miser is more excusable than the oppressor.” So he said to him:

“You have lied. Indeed, the oppressor may repent, seek forgiveness, and restore the wrong to its people. But the miser, when he is miserly, withholds zakat, charity, maintaining kinship ties, hospitality to the guest, spending in the way of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the doors of goodness; and it is forbidden for Paradise that a miser should enter it.”

key_terms.الشَّحِيحُ: the miserly person who withholds wealth and acts of goodness
key_terms.الظَّالِمَ: the oppressor or wrongdoer who violates the rights of others
key_terms.الظُّلَامَةَ: the wrong, usurped right, or injustice that must be restored
key_terms.الْجَنَّةِ: Paradise, the abode of reward in the afterlife
key_terms.يَتُوبُ: repents and turns back from wrongdoing

ai.seo_question: Why does Imam Ali عليه السلام say that a miser is not more excusable than an oppressor?
ai.summary: This hadith teaches that miserliness is not a light fault, because it blocks many obligations and virtues at once, including zakat, charity, kinship, and hospitality. Amir al-Mu'minin عليه السلام contrasts it with oppression, which may still be followed by tawbah, seeking forgiveness, and restoration of rights. The narration warns that entrenched greed cuts a person off from the pathways of righteousness and endangers entry into Paradise.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications:
Hadith.1718 - The Commander of the Faithful Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib (as) heard a man saying, "The miser is more excusable than the oppressor."
He said to him:

"You have lied. Indeed, the oppressor may repent, seek forgiveness, and restore the injustice to its rightful owners. But the miser, when he becomes miserly, withholds zakat, charity, maintaining family ties, hospitality to guests, spending in the way of Allah (swt), the Mighty and Majestic, and other acts of goodness. It is forbidden for a miser to enter Paradise."
